subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Introduction to Ecology and Levels of Organization

subjective.topic: Introduction to Ecology and Levels of Organization
subjective.question: Define ecology. Distinguish between autecology and synecology.
subjective.answer: Ecology is the scientific study of the interactions between organisms and their environment. The word is derived from the Greek 'oikos' (house or environment) and 'logos' (study). Autecology is the branch of ecology in which an individual's life history, behaviour and adaptation to the environment is studied, i.e. it deals with a single species. Synecology is the branch in which a group of organisms of different species associated together as a unit (a community) is studied in relation to the environment.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Ecology and Levels of Organization
subjective.question: Define an ecosystem and describe its biotic and abiotic components.
subjective.answer: An ecosystem is the community of living organisms together with the nonliving environment functioning as a unit; its biotic and abiotic components are interrelated and inseparable. Biotic components include producers (green plants), consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) and decomposers. Abiotic components include light, temperature, water, soil, air and inorganic nutrients.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Ecology and Levels of Organization
subjective.question: What is a biome? Give its main characteristics and examples.
subjective.answer: A biome is a large regional set of ecosystems characterized by uniform life forms such as vegetation, grasses, desert plants and trees, under a particular climate. Examples are the tundra, boreal coniferous forest, temperate deciduous forest, tropical rain forest, grassland and desert biomes.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Ecology and Levels of Organization
subjective.question: Define population and community. What is a species?
subjective.answer: A population is the group of organisms of the same species living in a particular geographic area at the same time, with the capability of interbreeding. A community consists of all the populations of different species that live and interact in a certain area. A discrete group of organisms of the same kind is called a species.

subjective.topic: Introduction to Ecology and Levels of Organization
subjective.question: Explain homeostasis with an example.
subjective.answer: Homeostasis is the tendency of a system to maintain its internal conditions despite all the fluctuations in the external environment. For example, animals regulate their body temperature, and water and salt balance, within narrow limits even when external conditions change, so that their internal environment remains nearly constant.

subjective.question: Differentiate between gross primary productivity and net primary productivity.
subjective.answer: Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total rate at which radiation energy is stored by photosynthesis in green plants. Net primary productivity (NPP) is the energy actually stored in plant tissues after the loss due to respiration, i.e. NPP = GPP - respiration. NPP represents the food available for consumers.

subjective.question: Define a food chain and a food web. Give one example of a food chain.
subjective.answer: A food chain is the linear sequence of organisms through which energy and nutrients pass, e.g. Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk. A food web is the graphical description of the feeding relationships among species in an ecological community; it is a network of many interconnected food chains, because most animals feed on more than one type of organism.

subjective.question: Classify consumers into different categories with examples.
subjective.answer: Consumers are heterotrophs that feed on other organisms. They are classified as: (1) Primary consumers - herbivores feeding directly on producers, e.g. deer, cow. (2) Secondary consumers - small carnivores feeding on herbivores, e.g. catfish, whales and sharks. (3) Tertiary consumers - larger carnivores feeding on secondary consumers, e.g. tiger. (4) Quaternary consumers - top carnivores feeding on tertiary consumers, e.g. hawk.

subjective.question: Write a note on scavengers and omnivores as special feeding groups.
subjective.answer: Scavengers are animals that feed on dead plants and animals, e.g. hyena and crow. The crow is a special feeder because it is a herbivore, a carnivore and also a scavenger, i.e. an omnivore. Scavengers clean the environment by removing carcasses and help return nutrients to the ecosystem.

subjective.question: What are decomposers? Differentiate between micro-decomposers and macro-decomposers with examples.
subjective.answer: Decomposers break down dead organic matter and release nutrients back into the ecosystem. Micro-decomposers are microscopic, e.g. bacteria and fungi. Macro-decomposers are larger organisms, e.g. shrimp. Detritivores are organisms which break down detritus into small particles, preparing it for further decomposition by bacteria and fungi.

subjective.question: Define symbiosis. Explain mutualism, commensalism and parasitism with examples.
subjective.answer: Symbiosis is an interspecific interaction in which two species live together in a long term intimate association. Its types include: (1) Mutualism - both species have a net benefit, e.g. lichens, the association of algae and fungus in which the algae prepares food and the fungus provides shelter and moisture. (2) Commensalism - one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed, e.g. sucker fish (remora) attached to a shark. (3) Parasitism - one species (parasite) benefits at the expense of the other (host).

subjective.question: What are lichens? Why are they important in ecological succession?
subjective.answer: Lichens are the association between algae and fungus living together in a mutualistic relationship. The algal partner photosynthesizes and provides food, while the fungal partner absorbs water and minerals and gives protection. Lichens are pioneer organisms: they are the first to colonize bare rocks and start primary succession by helping in soil formation.

subjective.question: What is resource partitioning? Explain it with the help of the warbler example.
subjective.answer: Resource partitioning is the division of limited resources by species to help avoid competition. For example, the different warbler species get their resources from different spots on the same tree by not occupying the same niche - each species feeds in a different part of the tree, so they coexist without direct competition.

subjective.question: Differentiate between crude density and ecological density. What is carrying capacity?
subjective.answer: Crude density is the number of population per unit of total space. Ecological density is the number of population per unit of habitat space, i.e. the actual area where the population lives. Ecological density is more meaningful because organisms do not occupy the whole area uniformly. The population size that a particular environment can support is called the environment's carrying capacity.

subjective.question: List and briefly explain the properties of a community.
subjective.answer: The properties of a community include species richness (the number of species present), species evenness (the relative abundance of each species), species area effect (species number increases with area), dominance, diversity and stratification. Allopatric speciation is not a property of a community; it is a process of formation of new species due to geographical isolation.

subjective.question: What is ecological succession? Differentiate between primary and secondary succession. Which community has the highest species diversity and why?
subjective.answer: Ecological succession is the gradual, directional change in the composition of a community in an area until a stable climax community is established. Succession beginning on a bare, lifeless area is primary succession, while that on a previously occupied, disturbed area is secondary succession. The climax community has high species diversity because, after a long succession, many species of plants and animals have colonized the area, food webs become complex, and niches are fully occupied, which makes the community stable and diverse.

subjective.question: What are biogeochemical cycles? Describe the important steps of the carbon cycle.
subjective.answer: Biogeochemical cycles are the processes that involve the cyclic movement of nutrients between the biotic and abiotic environment of the earth, e.g. carbon cycle, nitrogen cycle and water cycle. The carbon cycle has four important steps: (1) Photosynthesis - green plants fix atmospheric carbon dioxide into food. (2) Respiration - organisms release carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. (3) Decomposition - decomposers break down dead bodies and release carbon compounds. (4) Combustion - burning of fossil fuels and wood releases carbon dioxide. Oceans also contain large quantities of dissolved carbon dioxide and bicarbonates, which regulate the cycle.

subjective.question: Describe the distribution of water on the earth.
subjective.answer: Water is distributed very unevenly on the earth. Nearly 97.3% of the total water is in the oceans, and 2.1% exists as polar ice caps, which are the world's second largest reservoirs of water. The remaining small fraction is present as groundwater, lakes, rivers and water vapours in the atmosphere. Human activities tend to increase the rate of runoff, reducing the water available for groundwater recharge.

subjective.question: Define limnology. Differentiate between lentic and lotic water bodies with examples.
subjective.answer: Limnology is the study of freshwater. Lentic water bodies are standing water bodies, e.g. lake, pond and swamps. Lotic water bodies are flowing water bodies, e.g. rivers, springs and streams. Seas are not lotic water bodies.

subjective.question: Differentiate between torpor and hibernation.
subjective.answer: Torpor is a short-term state in which an animal lowers its metabolic activity and body temperature for a short duration only, e.g. during a cold night. Hibernation is a seasonal heterothermy characterized by low body temperature, slow breathing and heart rate, and low metabolic rate, lasting for the whole winter season (winter sleep). Unlike torpor, hibernation is not associated with higher metabolic activity at any stage.

subjective.question: Describe the location, climate and fauna of temperate deciduous forests.
subjective.answer: Temperate deciduous forests are mainly located in the middle latitudes of the Northern hemisphere. They have a moderate climate with four distinct seasons and broad-leaved trees that shed their leaves in autumn. Important animals include deer, rodents - which play an important role in these forests - wild cat, wolf and sparrow. The skunk is an omnivore found in these forests, while the cardinal belongs to the birds.

subjective.question: Why is the soil of boreal coniferous forest acidic in nature? Where are tropical rain forests well developed in India?
subjective.answer: The soil of boreal coniferous forest is acidic in nature because the fallen needles of coniferous trees decompose slowly and release acids, and the cold climate slows down decomposition and leaching of bases. In India, tropical rain forests are well developed over the western coast (Western Ghats) and the North Eastern Himalayas, where rainfall is very high.

subjective.question: How does the tsetse fly affect the distribution of cattle in Africa?
subjective.answer: The tsetse fly transmits sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis) to cattle in Africa. Because of this disease, cattle cannot be kept in the tsetse-infested regions, so the fly controls and limits the distribution of cattle over large areas of Africa. This shows how a single biotic factor can determine the distribution of a species.
